title: Route cards by an account-range file

blocks.text: Your switch's processor sends its routing table as an account-range file instead of a list of prefixes. Each row gives the first and the last eight-digit card prefix of a range, both included, and the destination for the cards in it. A bank's own range may sit inside a network's range. The file arrives every night and is put into service while authorizations keep coming.
Finish the three methods marked `TODO` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/RangeRouter.java`:

items: `holds`: whether a card belongs to a range;
`destinationFor`: where a card goes, or `null` when no range holds it;
`reload`: puts a newly parsed file into service.

blocks.text: When you're done, the bank's own cards reach its own host, every card at the edge of a range is routed by that range, and no lookup ever sees a file that is half read. About twelve lines in total.

cases.says: a card goes to the destination of the range that holds it, and a reloaded file replaces the old one
when ranges nest, the most specific one decides, whatever the order of the file's rows
the first and the last prefix of a row both belong to its range
a loaded table is the router's own copy, replaced whole, so a change to the parser's list does not reach it

origin.section: 11.2. A Card Goes to the Destination of Its Longest Matching Prefix

concepts: A card goes to the destination of the most specific entry that holds it, whatever the entry's length or its place in the table.
Routing tables are kept in memory and replaced whole, so a lookup sees one version of the table.
